items.q: Under the Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group India (DIPSI) guidelines, what is the single-step diagnostic threshold for gestational diabetes mellitus using a 75 g oral glucose challenge administered non-fasting?
items.exp: The DIPSI diagnostic guideline is an approved, non-fasting single-step test suitable for universal screening: 75 g of oral glucose is administered irrespective of the timing of the last meal, and a 2-hour venous plasma glucose >= 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) is diagnostic of gestational diabetes mellitus.
r: Correct. A 2-hour plasma glucose >= 140 mg/dL on the DIPSI test confirms GDM.
Incorrect. 180 mg/dL is the 1-hour threshold on fasting IADPSG testing.
Incorrect. Fasting >= 126 mg/dL diagnoses overt pre-existing diabetes.
Incorrect. 200 mg/dL is the threshold for overt diabetes mellitus.
items.kp: DIPSI criteria diagnose GDM when 2-hour venous plasma glucose is >= 140 mg/dL following a non-fasting 75 g oral glucose load.

items.q: Which placental hormone is primarily responsible for the progressive peripheral insulin resistance observed in maternal tissues during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy?
o: Human placental lactogen (hPL / human chorionic somatomammotropin)
items.exp: Human placental lactogen (hPL), also called human chorionic somatomammotropin (hCS), synthesized by the syncytiotrophoblast, is the primary anti-insulin hormone of pregnancy. It stimulates maternal lipolysis and downregulates peripheral insulin receptors, sparing glucose and amino acids for shunting to the growing fetus.
r: Correct. Human placental lactogen (hPL) is the primary anti-insulin hormone causing maternal insulin resistance.
Incorrect. hCG peaks at 10 weeks and stimulates the corpus luteum and thyroid.
Incorrect. Relaxin softens the cervix and pelvic ligaments.
Incorrect. Alkaline phosphatase is an enzyme, not a diabetogenic hormone.
items.kp: Human placental lactogen (hPL) is the primary hormone driving maternal insulin resistance in pregnancy.

items.q: What are the recommended target blood glucose levels for a woman with gestational diabetes on medical nutrition therapy?
o: Fasting < 95 mg/dL and 1-hour postprandial < 140 mg/dL (or 2-hour < 120 mg/dL)
items.exp: According to ACOG and ADA guidelines, optimal glycemic targets in GDM are: fasting blood glucose < 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L), 1-hour postprandial blood glucose < 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L), and 2-hour postprandial blood glucose < 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L).
r: Correct. Target fasting < 95 mg/dL and 1-hour postprandial < 140 mg/dL minimizes macrosomia risks.
Incorrect. Fasting up to 120 mg/dL allows significant hyperglycemia that drives fetal overgrowth.
Incorrect. Fasting < 70 mg/dL risks maternal neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.
Incorrect. Targets are too loose.
items.kp: Glycemic targets in GDM are fasting < 95 mg/dL and 1-hour postprandial < 140 mg/dL.

items.q: Why do neonates born to mothers with poorly controlled gestational diabetes exhibit a significantly higher incidence of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) even at near-term gestational ages?
o: Elevated fetal insulin levels antagonize the stimulatory effect of cortisol on surfactant synthesis
Insulin causes structural malformation of the tracheal cartilage
Maternal glucose blocks fetal alveolar fluid reabsorption
items.exp: Fetal hyperinsulinemia (resulting from maternal hyperglycemia) directly inhibits the transcription of surfactant proteins (specifically SP-A and SP-B) in type II alveolar pneumocytes and blocks the maturation signal normally mediated by endogenous fetal cortisol, leading to delayed surfactant synthesis and RDS.
r: Correct. Fetal hyperinsulinemia directly antagonizes cortisol-mediated pulmonary surfactant synthesis in type II pneumocytes.
Incorrect. Insulin does not cause tracheal malformations.
Incorrect. Fetal hyperinsulinemia, not glucose, mediates delayed lung maturation.
Incorrect. Neonates of diabetic mothers experience hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.
items.kp: Fetal hyperinsulinemia directly inhibits surfactant production in type II pneumocytes, increasing the risk of neonatal RDS.

items.q: A pregnant woman with pre-existing primary hypothyroidism controlled on 100 mcg daily of levothyroxine confirms a positive pregnancy test at 5 weeks gestation. What advice should be given regarding her levothyroxine dosing?
o: Immediately increase the daily dose by approximately 30% (e.g., take two extra tablets per week)
Stop levothyroxine immediately due to teratogenicity
Decrease the dose by 50% as estrogen lowers thyroid requirements
Maintain the exact same dose until the third trimester
items.exp: Pregnancy induces a dramatic increase in thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) and increased placental deiodinase degradation of thyroxine. In women with pre-existing hypothyroidism, endogenous thyroid reserve is absent, and levothyroxine requirements increase by 30% to 50% starting as early as 4 to 6 weeks. Patients are advised to immediately take two extra doses per week.
r: Correct. Levothyroxine requirements increase by 30-50% in early pregnancy; dosing must be increased immediately.
Incorrect. Levothyroxine is an essential physiological hormone, safe and mandatory in pregnancy.
Incorrect. Estrogen increases TBG, increasing the requirement for thyroxine.
Incorrect. Delaying dose adjustment risks maternal hypothyroidism and impaired fetal neurodevelopment.
items.kp: Levothyroxine requirements increase by 30% to 50% in early pregnancy; dosing must be increased immediately upon pregnancy confirmation.

items.q: What is the single most specific congenital malformation associated with pre-gestational maternal diabetes mellitus with poor peri-conceptional glycemic control (HbA1c > 10%)?
items.exp: While congenital cardiac defects (VSD, transposition of the great arteries) are the most common anomalies overall, caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis / sirenomelia) is the most specific anomaly for diabetic embryopathy, occurring with an odds ratio > 200 to 400 times higher in poorly controlled diabetic pregnancies than in the general population.
r: Correct. Caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis) is the most specific congenital anomaly associated with maternal diabetes.
Incorrect. VSD is the most common anomaly overall, but less specific.
Incorrect. Anencephaly is increased in diabetes, but not pathognomonically specific.
Incorrect. Duodenal atresia is strongly associated with Down syndrome.
items.kp: Caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis) is the most specific congenital anomaly associated with pre-gestational diabetes.

items.q: What is the primary pharmacological agent of choice when medical nutrition therapy fails to achieve glycemic targets in gestational diabetes?
items.exp: Insulin remains the gold-standard, first-line pharmacological treatment of choice for gestational diabetes worldwide. Insulin does not cross the placental barrier, carries zero teratogenicity, and allows precise dose titration to achieve strict glycemic targets without exposing the fetus to drug metabolites.
r: Correct. Insulin is the first-line pharmacotherapy for GDM because it does not cross the placenta.
Incorrect. Metformin crosses the placenta freely; it is acceptable in selected settings but second-line to insulin in major guidelines.
Incorrect. Sulfonylureas cross the placenta and can cause profound neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.
Incorrect. Thiazolidinediones are contraindicated in pregnancy.
items.kp: Insulin is the first-line medication for gestational diabetes because it does not cross the placenta.

items.q: A newborn delivered to a mother with gestational diabetes becomes jittery, irritable, and has poor feeding at 2 hours of life. Bedside capillary glucose is 28 mg/dL. What is the immediate treatment of choice?
o: Immediate breastfeeding or formula feeding; if symptomatic or < 25 mg/dL, intravenous 10% dextrose bolus (2 mL/kg) followed by continuous infusion
items.exp: Neonatal hypoglycemia (< 40 mg/dL) occurs in up to 25-40% of infants of diabetic mothers due to hyperplastic beta-cells continuing high insulin secretion after maternal glucose delivery ceases. Symptomatic hypoglycemia or glucose < 25 mg/dL requires prompt IV bolus of 10% dextrose (2 mL/kg over 5-10 minutes) followed by continuous glucose infusion (6-8 mg/kg/min).
r: Correct. Immediate feeding and IV 10% dextrose bolus followed by maintenance infusion is the protocol for neonatal hypoglycemia.
Incorrect. Glucagon is second-line if IV access fails.
Incorrect. Oral 50% dextrose is hyperosmolar and dangerous to neonatal mucosa.
Incorrect. Insulin would cause fatal worsening of hypoglycemia.
items.kp: Symptomatic neonatal hypoglycemia is treated with an IV bolus of 10% dextrose (2 mL/kg) followed by continuous infusion.

items.q: Why does transient gestational thyrotoxicosis occur frequently in women with severe hyperemesis gravidarum during the first trimester?
o: Markedly elevated hCG shares structural homology with TSH and cross-stimulates thyroid TSH receptors
Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland by thyroid peroxidase antibodies
Excessive maternal ingestion of iodine in prenatal vitamins
items.exp: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) shares an identical alpha-subunit with TSH and exhibits weak structural affinity for the TSH receptor. In the first trimester, particularly in conditions with massive hCG surges (hyperemesis gravidarum, molar pregnancy, multiple gestation), extremely high hCG levels cross-react with TSH receptors, transiently suppressing TSH and elevating free T4 without thyroid autoimmunity.
r: Correct. High hCG cross-stimulates thyroid TSH receptors due to structural homology, transiently suppressing TSH.
Incorrect. Graves disease involves thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI), absent in gestational thyrotoxicosis.
Incorrect. Iodine ingestion is not the driving mechanism.
Incorrect. TSH is suppressed, not elevated by an adenoma.
items.kp: Transient gestational thyrotoxicosis in hyperemesis gravidarum results from high hCG cross-stimulating thyroid TSH receptors.

items.q: What is the recommended timing for postpartum glucose testing in women who had gestational diabetes to screen for persistent pre-diabetes or type 2 diabetes mellitus?
o: 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum
Random blood glucose on the day of hospital discharge
No testing is required unless the patient becomes pregnant again
items.exp: Women with gestational diabetes carry a 50% lifetime risk of developing overt type 2 diabetes mellitus. Guidelines recommend performing a 2-hour 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum using standard non-pregnant criteria to detect impaired fasting glucose, impaired glucose tolerance, or overt diabetes.
r: Correct. A 75 g OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum is standard to screen for persistent impaired glucose tolerance.
Incorrect. Immediate discharge testing is confounded by pregnancy resolution changes.
Incorrect. HbA1c at 2 weeks reflects third-trimester pregnancy erythrocyte turnover.
Incorrect. Long-term surveillance is essential due to high lifetime T2D conversion.
items.kp: A 75 g OGTT is recommended at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum to screen for persistent diabetes in women with GDM.
